sections.title: Visual Cortex & Higher Cortical Dysfunction
content: Nondominant lobe lesions: May cause dressing apraxia, constitutional apraxia, and spatial neglect.
Cortical blindness: Formed visual hallucinations.
Anton Syndrome: Denial of blindness.
Riddoch Phenomenon: Only moving visual targets are perceived.

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS: 3rd Nerve Palsy
content: Pupillary involvement may be the only sign of 3rd N palsy (Basal meningitis, Uncal herniation)
Painful 3rd nerve palsy: Rule out PCoA Aneurysm immediately
Uncal herniation: Secondary to subdural haematoma

sections.title: 4th Nerve Palsy: Clinical Features & Compensations
content: Idiopathic: Often congenital
Trauma: Most common cause of bilateral 4th N palsy
Microvascular / Aneurysm / Tumor: Less common causes
Contralateral Head Tilt: To the right (if left palsy) to compensate for weakness of intorsion
Chin Depression: To alleviate weakened depression of the eye
Face Turn: Slightly to the right (if left palsy) as weakness is most marked in adduction

sections.title: Diagnosis of Bilateral 4th Nerve Palsy
content: Right hypertropia in left gaze
Left hypertropia in right gaze
Cyclodeviation > 10 degrees (measured via Double Maddox Rods or Synoptophore)
V-pattern Esotropia
Bilateral positive Bielschowsky head tilt test

sections.title: Park's Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify the hypertropic eye in primary position. This implicates either the depressors of the elevated eye (SO/IR) or elevators of the hypotropic eye (SR/IO).
Step 2: Determine if deviation is worse in right or left gaze. This assigns weakness to the two muscles having the greatest vertical action in that position.
Step 3: Hypertropia in head tilt. Assess muscle responsible for cyclotorsion when the patient is fixed on a target at 3m with head tilt to either side.

rows: Symmetrical recession of both Inferior Rectus muscles

branches: Foville Syndrome: Inferior medial pontine. Ipsilateral 5th, 8th, central sympathetic (Horner), horizontal gaze palsy.
Millard-Gubler Syndrome: Ventral pontine. Ipsilateral 6th N palsy (fasciculus), LMNL facial N palsy, contralateral hemiplegia (pyramidal tract).
Raymond Syndrome: Ipsilateral 6th N palsy, contralateral hemiplegia (pyramidal tract involvement).
Gradenigo Syndrome: Mastoiditis/acute petrositis. Damage to 6th N at petrous tip. Symptoms: 6th N palsy, 7th N weakness, pain, hearing difficulty.
Intracavernous 6th N Palsy: Damage to 6th N and paracarotid sympathetic plexus (Horner syndrome).
Parkinson Syndrome: (Listed in input context of base of skull/pontine)

sections.title: Facial Nerve (CN VII) Disorders
content: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome: Reactivation of Herpes Zoster in geniculate ganglion. Ear pain, vesicles on face/ear.
Causes: Bell's palsy, Trauma, Viral infection, Lyme disease, Neoplastic, Diabetes, Sarcoidosis.
Stroke Mimics: Hemiparesis/facial drooping caused by hypoglycaemia (elderly), migraine, sepsis, transient focal neuro signs.

sections.title: Management of Facial Nerve Palsy
content: 1. Corneal protection (Essential)
2. Corticosteroids: Prednisolone 60-80mg daily for 1 week (started within 48-72h), then taper over 1 week.
3. Antivirals: Acyclovir or Valaciclovir.
4. Neuroimaging: MRI scan of the brain.
5. If Bilateral: Chest X-ray and ACE levels to exclude Sarcoidosis.
6. Surgery (if indicated).

sections.title: Supranuclear Control of Eye Movements
sections.content: Saccades are initiated in the premotor cortex frontal eye fields; each lobe initiates contralateral saccades. Impulses for horizontal movement pass to the contralateral PPRF. Smooth pursuits pathway is complex, involving the cortex, PPRF, and superior colliculus. Pursuit palsy results from damage/hyperactivity in the parietoccipital lobe, causing unilateral pursuit palsy in the ipsilateral direction.

sections.title: Parinaud (Dorsal Midbrain) Syndrome
content: Signs: Straight eye in primary position.
Supranuclear upgaze/downgaze palsy in saccadic movement.
Defective convergence.
Normal downgaze using doll’s head manoeuvre.
Large pupils with light-near dissociation.
Collier Sign: Lid retraction.
Convergence-retraction nystagmus.
Causes (Children): Aqueduct stenosis, meningitis, pinealoma.
Causes (Young Adults): Demyelination, trauma, AVM.
Causes (Elderly): Midbrain vascular accidents, mass lesions, periaqueductal grey matter, posterior fossa aneurysms.

sections.title: Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Workup & Management
content: Investigations: Ice pack test, Edrophonium (Tensilon) test, Electromyography, Muscle biopsy.
Antibody Testing: AChR antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies, Striational antibodies (severe marker), Voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies (Lambert-Eaton).
Imaging: Thoracic CT/MRI/PET (Thymoma/Lung tumor), Thyroid function testing.
Treatment: Pyridostigmine + Steroids/Azathioprine.
Acute/Short-term: Plasmapheresis and IVIG.
Surgical: Thymectomy.
Emergency: Respiratory support.

sections.title: Kearns-Sayre Syndrome: Clinical Details
content: Etiology: Mitochondrial DNA deletion; Cerebral folate deficiency.
Onset: 1st-2nd decades (Sporadic).
Systemic: Fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, deafness, diabetes, cerebellar ataxia, short stature, renal disease, dementia.
Histology: Ragged red fibres (intramuscular accumulation of abnormal mitochondria).
Screening: Genetic testing, ECG, Endocrine screening.

sections.title: Ocular Surface Oncology: Conjunctival & Iris Lesions
content: Malignant Conjunctival Nevus signs: Unusual site (palpebral/forniceal), prominent feeder vessels, sudden growth, increased pigmentation, development after 2nd decade.
Conjunctival Melanoma Poor Prognosis: Caruncle/forniceal/lid margin location, thickness >= 2mm.
Iris Nevus Risk Factors: Age <40y, inferior location, bleeding, diffuse involvement, feathery margin, ectropion uvae.

sections.title: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN)
content: Risk Factors: UV light, pale complexion, Ciclosporin, Smoking, Petroleum exposure, AIDS, Xeroderma pigmentosum, HPV Type 16.
Investigations: UBM, AS-OCT, Exfoliative/Impression cytology.
Treatment: Excision with 2-4mm margins (do not cut below Bowman's).
Adjunctive: Cryotherapy, Brachytherapy, Topical Chemo, Subconjunctival Interferon.
Limbal Dermoid Associations: Goldenhar, Treacher Collins, Linear naevus sebaceous of Jadassohn.

sections.title: Role of Topical Chemotherapy in OSSN
content: A. Avoid recurrence & stem cell damage.
B. Reduce tumour size prior to excision.
C. Treat recurrence.
Regimen: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) 4x daily for 1 week, followed by 3 weeks rest.
Other agents: Topical Interferon Alfa-2b, Mitomycin C.
